properties.description: Weitere Informationen erhalten Sie [hier](https://haus-lutherrose.de/preise/raeumlichkeiten/).

properties.name: Kaspar Hauser Monument
properties.description:
Friedrich Schelle took up an idea by the Ansbach sculptor Waldemar Fritsch and created the bronze figures. Kaspar Hauser is depicted twice: the bent figure shows him as he might have appeared when he emerged in Nuremberg on May 26, 1828; the well-dressed, upright man gives an impression of how he was summoned into the courtyard garden by his murderer on December 14, 1833. Between the figures lies a bronze plaque shaped like a sheet of paper.

It bears a text by Friedrich Schiller:
THEY HAVE IN VAIN
WAGED THE HARD STRUGGLE
WITH NATURE,
IN VAIN SACRIFICED GREAT ROYAL
LIFE-DESTROYING DESIGNS.
MAN IS MORE
THAN YOU HAVE HELD HIM TO BE,
HE WILL BREAK THE BONDS
OF LONG SLUMBER AND DEMAND AGAIN
HIS SACRED RIGHT

properties.name: Flute Player
properties.description:
In the little Baroque garden behind the inn “Zum Mohren,” the flute player has been playing merrily for several years.

Since the beginning of his artistic career, the flute player has been a recurring motif in Ernst Steinacker’s work.

The Ansbach flute player sits with his legs crossed, above which his arms rise in a sweeping motion, bringing the flute to life in the play of his fingers.

Body, sound, and soul unite into a sculpted whole.

And sometimes in summer, the flute player has picked a little flower, which he holds between his fingers.

The figure was donated by the former mayor of the city of Ansbach, Dr. Ernst-Günther Zumach.

properties.name: Resting on the Stone
properties.description:
Seit vielen Jahren liegt die anmutige Gestalt einer jungen Frau wie hingegossen im Schatten eines Geldinstituts.

Die lebensgroße Bronzeplastik „Ruhende auf dem Stein“ war schon 1978 in einer Ausstellung in der Karlshalle zu sehen.

Der Künstler Kurt Moser hatte sich den Ansbachern als einer der wenigen zeitgenössischen Künstler vorgestellt, die Mut zu naturalistischen Darstellungen hatten.

properties.name: Mission EineWelt - BegegnungsCentrum Neuendettelsau
properties.description: Nähere Informationen erhalten Sie [hier](https://begegnungscentrum-neuendettelsau.de/tagungen-gruppenangebote/).

properties.name: Der Drachenkämpfer
properties.description:
Die rund zwei Meter hohe Eichenholzskulptur entstand 1997 während eines Symposiums für Skulpturisten in Ansbach. Fünf Künstler aus Russland, Japan und Deutschland fertigten in rund einem Monat Kunstwerke, die von Sponsoren erworben wurden.

Zum 1250-jährigen Stadtjubiläum schenkte ein Sponsor der Stadt den „Drachenkämpfer“, der nach verschiedenen Stationen seinen Platz im Foyer des Tagungszentrums Onoldia fand.

Der 1959 geborene Prowatorow lehnte seine Skulptur vermutlich an den Heiligen Georg, den Schutzpatron Moskaus, an. Der getötete Drache wurde in ein Schiff umgewandelt, auf dem der Heilige steht. Mit der Skulptur hat sich der Künstler in die Zeit des frühen Mittelalters zurückversetzt und eingefühlt.

properties.name: St. Gumbertus Sculpture
properties.description: Auf einem Sockel oberhalb der Rezatbrücke wurde im Jubliäumsjahr 1998 (1250 Jahre Ansbach) die Bronzeskulptur des Heiligen Gumbertus installiert. St. Gumbertus gilt als Klostergründer und somit als „Vater“ der Ansiedlung. Die Skulptur weist ein hohes Maß an Symbolik auf: Der überlebensgroße Gumbertus ist kein kriegerischer Edelmann, sondern ein älterer, gereifter Mann und Mönch. Seinen Mantel hält eine Brosche, die ein Kreuz zeigt und ihm im Wortsinn am Herzen liegt. Eine Schrifttafel unweit der Statue vertieft diesen Gedanken. Die vom Künstler gewählten Bibelworte spielen mit den Begriffen „Schwert des Glaubens, Rüstung und Schild“. Die runde Tafel symbolisiert den abgelegten Schild des Kriegers, als er diesen gegen die Rüstung des Glaubens tauschte, und das abgelegte Schwert, das in Kreuzform die Tafel teilt. Links findet sich in Negativ-Lettern die weltliche Stellung Gumbertus‘ und seine Vergangenheit, rechts in erhabener Schrift seine künftige geistliche Funktion. Folgt man dem schmalen Weg hinauf zur Skulptur, schweift der Blick weit in die Stadt hinein bis zu den Türmen von St. Gumbertus, wo der Klostergründer im 8. Jahrhundert wirkte.

properties.name: Ernst von Bandel
properties.description: Hinter dem Museum direkt an der ehemaligen Stadtmauer findet sich eine Skulptur von Ernst von Bandel. Der Sohn der Stadt Ansbach hat die Kolossalstatue des Hermannsdenkmals entworfen. Aus Anlass des 40-jährigen Jubiläums des Lions-Club Ansbach, der die Skulptur gestiftet hat, wurde das Denkmal am 24. September 2011 eingeweiht. Das Bandel-Denkmal ist in Kupfer gegossen. Es zeigt Bandel gleichsam „durch den Schleier der Geschichte“, der in der geriffelten Oberfläche der Figur zum Ausdruck kommt. Der Künstler sieht Bandel als einen Mann des 19. Jahrhunderts und demonstriert diese zeitliche Distanz zum Heute in der Plastik. In ihrer Abstraktion der körperlichen Form zeigt die Figur den Bildhauer als wuchtige, zugleich reduzierte Gestalt, die das Denkmal als einziges Zeugnis ihrer Arbeit hält; die Werkzeuge Bandels: Architektenzirkel, Schmiedehammer, Zimmermannsfeile, liegen zu seinen Füßen.

properties.name: Michael-Kirschner-Kulturmuseum
properties.description: Eine alte und eine neue Scheune sowie ein Wohnstallhaus bilden das Michael-Kirschner-Kulturmuseum. Mit ihrer originalen Ausstattung wie „anno dazumal“ erzählen sie vom einfachen Leben mit weitgehender Selbstversorgung auf dem Land.

properties.name: Lech and Malsche
properties.description:
Hier finden sich zwei große Köpfe mit Durchblick des Künstlers Jürgen Goertz, die sich aus der Ferne anhimmeln. Für „Lech“ stand der Fluss Lech Pate. Schädeldecke und Stirn sind wellenartig ausgeformt, Treibgut wird zum Haar, der Hinterkopf mutiert zur Welle. Die Augen schimmern tränenverhangen, die durchbrochene Nase endet in einer Muschelspitze und taucht in die weiche Oberlippenwelle. Der Mund schlürft Flüssiges, ein Ohr hört das Geräusch des fließenden Wassers, der Sockel ist gekerbt, bildet das Flussbett für den Wasserkopf und die Gießkannenbrause besiegelt die geschlechtliche Seite des Wassermannes.

Aus diesem Blickwinkel betrachtet, hört man die sanften Wellen eines Flusses regelrecht schwappen. Bei „Malsche“ strafen Proportionsverzerrungen gängige Schönheitserwartungen: wulstige Aufwerfungen und tiefe Schluchtungen stören die vertraute Massenordnung, Ohren sind nach unten verrutscht, Nasen wurden zu offenen Brücken zwischen Stirn und Lippen, Augen sind aus der Symmetrie geraten. En face fast modisch schön – im Profil desillusionierend naturfern.

Zwischen den beiden Skulpturen unter schattigem Blätterdach ein Spielbrunnen – im Sommer bei Kindern hoch im Kurs.

properties.name: Tagungszentrum Diakoneo Neuendettelsau
properties.description: 14 Tagungsräume sowie 2 große Säle, einer davon bietet Platz für bis zu 350 Personen bei Reihenbestuhlung.Tagungs- und Veranstaltungstechnik vorhanden.

properties.name: War memorial and memorial to the victims of the Second World War
properties.description:
On the south tower there is a war memorial dedicated in 1927 to those who died in the First World War. The inscription reads:
MCMXIV – MCMVIII
TO THEIR FALLEN SONS
THE GRATEFUL HOMELAND

Below it are the Christ monogram and Alpha and Omega. To the right and left are the reliefs of the death masks of two young men, created by Professor Waldemar Fritsch, commemorating the victims of the Second World War. Traditionally, wreaths are laid here every year on Remembrance Day.

properties.name: Zeitsprung
properties.description:
In the architecturally cohesive ensemble of Karlsplatz, the sculpture “Zeitsprung” has stood since 2011.

Here too, the symbiosis of modern art and historic building fabric has a very special effect.

The sculptor Rolf Szymanzski is always driven toward form.

Sometimes he happens upon small details that others would overlook or fail to notice.

These become sources of inspiration for him — whether it is a newspaper photo with the fragment of the shadow of a female figure on a wall, a horseshoe nail, or an Aramaic sandal in the Jerusalem Museum.

They take root, occupy the artist’s mind, and mature into a process of growth that defines his art.

Szymanzski’s figures convey the impression of ore frozen in flux, seem like snapshots, and span an impressive range of sizes.

properties.name: Margrave Karl Wilhelm Friedrich Fountain
properties.description:
On the flank of the Swan Knights' Chapel, the Margrave Karl Fountain has stood since 1746, as historians call it. The namesake is also the donor, who glorified his power with this fountain as well. The gilded bust is a replica of a marble bust in the Palace.

The inscription on the fountain basin reads:  
His Serene Highness, Carl Wilhelm Friedrich,  
Margrave of Brandenburg, Duke in Prussia  
and Silesia, Father of the Fatherland, who  
already adorned the city with many new buildings,  
also had this fountain built in 1746  
for the constant benefit of the inhabitants and  
for pleasant contemplation.

How wonderful that this “pleasant contemplation” is still possible today!

properties.name: Waben
properties.description: Seit 2022 steht das Werk, das aus 16 konisch zulaufenden sechseckigen Röhren besteht und sich zu einer Tropfen Form zusammensetzt, vor dem Amt in der Rügländerstraße, Ecke Mariusstraße. Als exakte Baumeister hexagonaler Formen, sind die Bienen Ideengeber der Plastik und die Schnittstelle der drei Amtsbereiche: Ernährung, Landwirtschaft und Forsten. Die Waben symbolisieren das existenzielle Thema der Nachhaltigkeit, zudem entsteht durch die ebenso geometrische wie organische Formensprache eine spannende Verbindung zwischen dem würfelförmigen Baukörper aus Holz und den bronzenen „Waben“.

properties.name: Platen Monument
properties.description:
AUGUST GRAF V. PLATEN HALLERMÜNDE GEBOREN IN ANSBACH XXIV OCTOBER MDCCXCVI GESTORBEN IN SYRACUS V. DEZEMBER DCCCXXXV.  
Seit dem 19. Jahrhundert (einer denkmalfreudigen Epoche) steht zu Ehren des Ansbacher Dichters August Graf von Platen sein Standbild auf dem Schlossplatz.

Eine mittlerweile imposant gewachsene Eibe, lässt Platen bescheiden in den Hintergrund treten. Die von Halbig modellierte und Miller gegossene Figur ist etwa drei Meter hoch und – eines Dichters würdig – mit Griffel und Buch ausgestattet.

Der Text auf dem Sockel lautet:  
UNTER DER REGIERUNG UND MIT  
BEITRAG MAXIMILIANS II KÖNIG VON  
BAYERN MIT DEM VON KÖNIG LUDWIG  
GESCHENKTEN ERZE ERRICHTET VON  
DEN FREUNDEN DES DICHTERS.

properties.name: Campus of Ansbach University of Applied Sciences
properties.description: Die *Hochschule Ansbach* wurde 1996 unter dem Namen *Fachhochschule Ansbach* gegründet.

properties.name: Horizontal Development
properties.description:
The sculptor Thomas Röthel lives and works near Ansbach. In 2004, he designed the Ansbach Sculpture Mile. One work of art remained in front of the town hall: “Horizontal Development.” Each of Röthel’s works stands on its own in the process, is its own model. Every beginning is the same and requires grappling with the hardness of the material. Cutting and bending are associated with the splitting and opening of the material. As if this intervention were releasing a hidden tension, the heavy mass can at that moment seem to strive with apparent ease into the horizontal or vertical, or return to its base. No part of the whole is lost.

Interestingly, this work of art also has practical uses: sometimes children use its slope as a slide, sometimes it serves as seating, and at festivities it is welcome as a surface for setting down glasses. But beware: in summer it gets very hot!

properties.name: Wolfgangshof Estate
properties.description: Über das Kontaktformular oder per E-Mail können Sie uns Ihre Wünsche mitteilen. Wir besprechen mit Ihnen die perfekte Lösung: event@faber-castell.de

properties.name: Erlangen Weekly Market
properties.description: Heute findet hier von Montag bis Samstag ein Wochenmarkt statt, wobei der Schwerpunkt auf dem Samstag liegt. Ob **Obst** über **Gemüse**, **Blumen** und **Pflanzen**, **Fleisch** und **Eier**, **Fisch** oder **Käse** und **Antipasti**, im Bauch von Erlangen ist der Einkaufskorb schnell gefüllt. Mehrere **Imbiss-Stände** bieten kleine Leckereien für die Mittagspause oder den Einkaufsbummel an. Kernzeiten für alle Händler: Montag bis Samstag, 9:00 bis 14:00 Uhr.

properties.name: Simon-Marius-Denkmal
properties.description: Hinter dem Schlosstor findet man ein interessantes Denkmal zum Ansbacher Mathematiker und Hofastronom Simon Marius (1573 – 1624), der 1609 die Jupitermonde entdeckt hatte. Bis heute steht in der Diskussion, ob Simon Marius oder Galileo Galilei zuerst die Entdeckung machte. Fest steht, dass der Ansbacher – sollte er denn die Nase vorn gehabt haben – es versäumte, seine Entdeckung zeitnah zu publizieren. Die runde Scheibe auf dem Boden zeigt die vier Monde und ihre Umlaufbahnen um den Planeten. Der Kopf stellt Simon Marius beim Blick in den Himmel dar. Das Kunstwerk wurde von Friedrich Schelle in München geschaffen und vom Lions-Club gestiftet. Klaus Goths Brunnen von 2002 und die drei Fische am Rand zieren auch das Ansbacher Stadtwappen.

properties.name: Asparago Grande
properties.description:
Die Skulpturenmeile 2017 wurde von den Künstlern Herbert Mehler und Thomas Röthel präsentiert, die beide mit mächtigen Stahlskulpturen beeindrucken.

Der „Große Spargel“ weist geschmeidige Linien und eine raue Oberfläche auf.

Stolz und zugleich elegant ragt er über drei Meter in die Höhe und schmückt den eleganten Straßenzug zwischen Herrieder Tor und dem eindrucksvollen historischen Gebäude-Ensemble an der „Steinernen Promenade“.

properties.name: Peace Stele
properties.description:
Above this are seven forged rings, which are as old as the Jewish cemetery, established in 1817. These rings connect the four sides. The number seven is a special number in all world religions. In Christianity, it stands for the creation of the world; in Islam, the seventh heaven is the final transfiguration reached by the Prophet Muhammad; in Judaism, it symbolizes abundance and wholeness; and in Buddhism it is the number of ascent, but also a symbol of joy, equanimity, mindfulness, and kindness.

As the artist said at the unveiling, the peace stele is meant to remind Jews and Christians, between the Jewish cemetery and the Catholic Church Christkönig, of peace and mutual respect.

properties.name: Man with Suitcase
properties.description:
The Swiss sculptor has a subtle sense of humor, which is also clearly perceptible in his sculptures.

The renowned artist has always found aesthetic solutions, whether in playing with asymmetries, with different encounters of materials, or with confusing sensory impressions.

In 2007, he equipped an interesting sculpture promenade with imposing large-scale sculptures.

Since then, the man with the suitcase has stood on the old town side of the bridge to the Brücken-Center.

The flâneur finds his counterpart on the other side.

properties.name: Margrave George Fountain
properties.description: Several misconceptions surround this fountain and its sculpture. Originally realized by the Margravial Councillor Dr. Pfotel through a donation to Margrave Casimir (1515), it was, through erroneous tradition, dedicated to Margrave George (reigned 1528–1543). It was renovated in 1780 and in the 19th century. And the figure that is supposed to depict Margrave George is in fact a representation of a knight in field armor from around 1500.

properties.name: Naga Instable
properties.description: An artist also came from Ansbach’s long-standing partner city to contribute to the Sculpture Mile in 2005: Claude Viseux. Unique in its design, complexity, and multi-part structure, the object found its place after several relocations; in honor of the partner city, it bears the name Anglet. Originally, the work — as the title suggests — was planned to be much more movable than it is in its final form.

properties.name: Steel sculpture
properties.description:
So unnachgiebig wie das Material, so unnachgiebig ist die Idee, die am Anfang jeder Arbeit des Stahlbildhauers Thomas Röthel steht.

Die Urform jeder Skulptur ist ein individuelles Ausgangsformat aus massivem Stahl industrieller Fertigung.

Einschnitte, Biegungen und Drehungen nutzt der Künstler, um die Form aus der Starre und der Schwerkraft zu lösen.

Sie wird in einen eigenständigen Ausdruck gewandelt, der die Härte und das Gewicht des Materials fast vergessen macht.

Nahe dem Tor zum Garten ist in der Mauer eine Relieftafel eingelassen, die den Leibarzt und Botaniker Leonhart Fuchs würdigt, der von 1528 – 1535 in Ansbach wirkte.

properties.name: Residenz Ansbach
properties.description:
Die Residenz Ansbach entwickelte sich aus einer mittelalterlichen Anlage. Sie ist ein beliebtes Ausflugsziel in Franken für alle Freunde schöner Schlösser. Ältester sichtbarer Gebäudeteil ist heute die sogenannte Gotische Halle aus der zweiten Hälfte des 16. Jahrhunderts mit ihrem Netzrippengewölbe, in der mit der „Sammlung Ansbacher Keramik Adolf Bayer“ der größte Bestand von Fayencen und Porzellan aus der ehemaligen Ansbacher Manufaktur ausgestellt ist. Zwischen 1705 und 1730 erfolgte der Umbau des Schlosses zu einer barocken Fürstenresidenz.  

Das Appartement des Markgrafen, das der Markgräfin und das Gästeappartement stellen ein beeindruckendes Zeugnis höfischer Wohnkultur dar.

Die außergewöhnlich gut erhaltene Innenausstattung entstand überwiegend zwischen 1734 und 1745 unter der Leitung des Architekten Leopoldo Retti. Seit der Abdankung des letzten Markgrafen 1791 blieb das Interieur nahezu unverändert – ein Glücksfall für die Nachwelt.

Zu den Höhepunkten zählen das Deckenfresko von Carlo Carlone im Festsaal, die Gemäldegalerie (Zweiggalerie der Bayerischen Staatsgemäldesammlungen) und feines Porzellan im funkelnden Spiegelkabinett. Eine besondere Rarität stellen die präparierten markgräflichen Pferde aus dem 18. Jahrhundert dar.

Heute ist die ehemalige Markgrafenresidenz Teil der Bayerischen Verwaltung der staatlichen Schlösser, Gärten und Seen und auch Sitz der Regierung von Mittelfranken. Die Prunkräume sind im Rahmen von Führungen, die Keramiksammlung in der Gotischen Halle auch individuell zu besichtigen.

Gruppen sowie Personen mit Einschränkungen bitte vorher anmelden.

Im gegenüberliegenden Hofgarten mit Orangerie laden ein repräsentatives Parterre im französischen Stil und zahlreiche Kübelpflanzen, die Lindenalleen sowie der Leonhart-Fuchs-Garten mit Heilkräutern und Nutzpflanzen zum Naturgenuss ein.

properties.name: Stadtschloss Herrieden
properties.description:
For conferences, two rooms and the Bürgerpark are available for rent.

The Relief Room can accommodate a maximum of 45 people, and the Council Chamber has approximately 170 seats with theater-style seating.

For fire safety reasons, the total capacity throughout the entire palace is limited to 200 people.

The Bürgerpark is open to the public and can be cordoned off for a fee upon request.

properties.name: Two Angels
properties.description: Der Standort dieser beiden anmutigen Engel im Schatten der Gumbertuskirche könnte idealer nicht sein. Ernst Steinacker begann Anfang der 1990er Jahre mit der Gestaltung großer Engelsskulpturen und Engelbilder. Auch in diesem Skulpturenpaar ist eine sinnliche, naturhafte Präsenz der Formenwelt des Künstlers gegenwärtig, die Sprache seines spirituellen Vorstellungsvermögens ist auf Essenzielles vereinfacht und in hoch aufragende, still erblühende Engelformen komponiert.

properties.name: Kaspar’s Tree
properties.description: Ihr Platz wurde mit Bedacht gewählt: zwischen dem ehemaligen Wohnhaus des Findlings Kaspar Hauser und dem ehemaligen Appellationsgericht, wo dieser als Schreiber tätig war. Die Plastik von Jaume Plensa wurde anlässlich des 1000-jährigen Jubiläums des Erzbistums Bamberg gestiftet. Die sitzende Kaspar-Hauser-Figur ist mit Worten überzogen, die einen Bezug zum menschlichen Körper haben. Wunsch des Künstlers war es, im Gedenken an Kaspar Hauser eine Skulptur zu schaffen, die ihren Platz in direkter Nähe des Wohn- und Sterbehauses findet. Der Mensch umfasst einen Baum, dessen Wandlungen symbolhaft für die stete Veränderung stehen.

properties.name: Pair of Flute Players
properties.description: In 2016, the small square next to the savings bank was officially named, and the pair of sculptures was unveiled. The slender flute players, with their pronounced physicality, suggest youthfulness in the harmony of a melody. Man and woman stand facing each other, and yet each of them is absorbed in their playing.

properties.name: Thinking Head
properties.description: On the east facade of the technical college, there is an impressive wire sculpture. The Thinking Head, here too in an interesting tension with the school and its students, was created by Gianfranco “Pico” Romagnoli from Fermo and was inaugurated and unveiled with the new school building in 2006. The Italian town of Fermo in the Marche has been Ansbach's partner city since 2006.

properties.name: Church site “St. Walburga" Muhr am See
properties.description: On Stadelnerstr. in Muhr am See, near Lake Altmühl in the Franconian Lake District, stands St. Walburga Church. It is dedicated to Saint Walburga, who lived in nearby Heidenheim am Hahnenkamm and is a founder of our diocese.

properties.name: Experience Faber-Castell
properties.description:
The Fascinating World of Faber-Castell

The ensemble of production facilities, representative buildings, and a landscape park, brought to life by Lothar von Faber and Alexander Count von Faber-Castell, is open to the public. The juxtaposition of the company’s past and future, family-run for over 250 years, is particularly fascinating.

Count von Faber-Castell Castle

Count von Faber-Castell Castle has been carefully restored in recent years and invites visitors on a tour where the connection between industrial progress and traditional family values can be experienced.

Museum "Old Mine"

At the “Old Mine” museum, visitors gain insight into the elaborate processes of pencil-making from the 19th century to the mid-20th century in the original, graphite-blackened rooms.

Production "Wood-Cased Pencils"

In the production of colored pencils and graphite pencils, over 500,000 wood-cased pencils are manufactured every day. During a two-hour guided tour, the production process is vividly presented and visitors learn how a finished pencil is made from a small wooden board.

Visitor Center and Shop

The 800-square-meter visitor center is the starting point for discovering the brand and the company’s history. The design of the space reflects the industrial Art Nouveau charm of the early 20th century and gives visitors a colorful insight into the world of Faber-Castell. A ceiling made of around 32,400 colored pencils in rainbow colors leads guests into the approximately 200-square-meter flagship store.

properties.name: Museum Bayerische Metallwarenfabrik - BMF (Museum Bavarian Metalware Factory)
properties.description: It is impossible to imagine today's gastronomy without the sugar shaker with the tube in the metal lid. And it is only one of numerous design classics that were produced at the Bayerische Metallwarenfabrik.From 1902 to 1998, the Bayerische Metallwarenfabrik was one of Nuremberg's most important metalworking companies. Product designs, company catalogues and numerous historical products take visitors on a journey through 100 years of table culture in the museum in the former factory building, where they are sure to meet one or two "acquaintances".

properties.name: Rathaus
properties.description:
A Touch of Florence in Fürth

Fürth Town Hall stands out clearly from its surroundings in terms of size and architecture. The building was constructed in the neoclassical style between 1840 and 1850. It reflects the self-confidence of the emerging industrial city and is located on the main thoroughfare, Königstraße. The Town Hall was modeled on the Palazzo Vecchio in Florence. The 52-meter-high square tower was fitted with 2,000 new LED lamps in 2018, which bathe Fürth's landmark in festive light on special occasions. The design of the building is characterized above all by round-arched windows, inspired by the early Italian Renaissance.

Due to the city's rapid growth, an extension was needed just 50 years later, and it is very similar to the main building. Today, this section houses the council chamber with its Neo-Renaissance furnishings. Wood paneling and an artistically decorated coffered ceiling give the room a dignified appearance.

Also well worth seeing is the neoclassical staircase with its marbled arcades. The elegant painting begins in dark tones at the base and becomes progressively lighter toward the delicate ceiling painting. The ceiling is decorated with leaf and foliage ornaments, with the three-leaf clover, Fürth's city symbol, at the center. This coat of arms can be found in many places throughout the building as a decorative element.

As part of the guided tour **Blickpunkt Rathaus, Turm und Co.**, you can explore the neoclassical administrative building and climb the tower.

Tip: If you are near the Town Hall around lunchtime, listen closely. Since 2007, the carillon in the Town Hall has played **"Stairway to Heaven" by Led Zeppelin** every day at 12:04 p.m. Alternatively, you can listen to it **[here](hier)**.

properties.name: Museum34
properties.description:
Museum34 is located in your 14th-century building.

The cellar resembles a mine tunnel, Auerbach's history is presented in a fascinating way, and changing permanent and special exhibitions round off the concept.

properties.name: Landl-Museum (Landl Museum)
properties.description: Das Landlmuseum zeigt neben Versteinerungen und archäologischen Funden landwirtschaftliche Werkzeuge und Geräte, Handwerk, Wohnungseinrichtung und „das Landl in alten Bildern und Urkunden“. Außerdem werden die Geschichte der Schlossherren, die Reichsgrafen von Wolfstein sowie unter dem Motto „Migration über Jahrhunderte“ das Zusammenleben der verschiedenen Kulturen und Religionen in Sulzbürg erzählt. Schule „anno dazumal“ darf natürlich nicht fehlen, denn das Museum ist im früheren protestantischen Schulhaus untergebracht.

properties.name: Walburga Chapel on the Walberla
properties.description:
The chapel was built as early as the 17th century. It is dedicated to Saint Walburga. The chapel, which was probably first mentioned in 1350, was initially built of wood. The present chapel was built in 1697 by the lords of Wiesenthau.

The bronze statue of Saint Walburga standing in front of the chapel, which was inaugurated in 2000, is particularly striking.

properties.name: Höhenschwimmbad Gößweinstein - Naturbad
properties.description:
The Gößweinstein High-Altitude Swimming Pool is an idyllically situated natural swimming area in the heart of Franconian Switzerland that captivates visitors with its nature-oriented design and biological water treatment. It offers a magnificent view of the basilica and Gößweinstein Castle and is a popular destination for those seeking relaxation.

The grounds, with their various terraces and bizarre-looking rock formations, offer a wide range of activities and unexpected enjoyment of nature. Since nature and chemicals don’t mix well, the Gößweinstein Mountain Swimming Pool is operated not as a conventional outdoor pool, but as a natural swimming area. The pool is purified by an efficient plant-based filtration system located in the regeneration area next to the pool. Thus, the focus of a visit to the Gößweinstein High-Altitude Swimming Pool is the pure experience of nature.

**Admission to the natural swimming pool is free. (Donations welcome). There are no lifeguards—swimming is at your own risk.**

The following facilities are also located nearby:

- Kneipp facility
- Mini-golf course
- 3D archery course
- Disc golf course

properties.name: Museumshof
properties.description: In the Museumshof (Museum yard), a 16th century farmhouse, visitors can look forward to historically designed rooms and objects from "grandmother's household" as well as old craft tools. In the barn cellar there is an archaeological section on the history of the Ottonian imperial palace of Roßtal.

properties.name: Market Square "Green Market" with Juggler Fountain
properties.description:
Once a trading route - today a lively meeting place

The Green Market was once the center of old Fürth. An important trading route ran here. After Fürth was almost completely destroyed in the Thirty Years' War in 1632, the surviving historic buildings around the Green Market, apart from St. Michael's Church, mostly date from the first half of the 17th century and the 18th century. Alongside simple half-timbered houses, there are sandstone buildings with Baroque curved gables that bear witness to the city's economic upswing in the 18th century. Particularly eye-catching is the Baroque former inn "Zum goldenen Schwan" with its artistically designed sign.

The market square itself is actually a widened street that, after an elaborate redesign, became the new small and lively city center. A special attraction is the "Juggler Fountain," designed by Harro Frey in 2004. The two groups of figures depict acrobats and performers and recall that many artists used to perform here in earlier times.

properties.name: Ossinger Tower in Königstein
properties.description: The 22-meter-high Ossinger Tower offers views of Franconia and across the Upper Palatinate.

properties.name: Saazer Heimatmuseum (Saaz Museum of Local History)
properties.description: In the small local history room, documents, books, photos and traditional costumes provide an insight into the life and development of the town and district of Saaz in Bohemia from the 13th to the 20th century.

properties.name: Klostermühlenmuseum Gnadenberg (Gnadenberg Monastery Mill Museum)
properties.description: Die Pfalzgräfin von Neumarkt gründete 1439 das erste Birgittenkloster Deutschlands am Eichelberg-Gnadenberg. Im Dreißigjährigen Krieg wurden das Kloster und die Klostermühle zerstört. Der nachfolgende Klostermüller baute 200 m weiter südlich an der Schwarzach eine neue Mühle. Der Kulturhistorische Verein und die Gemeinde Berg sanierten die durch ein Hochwasser zerstörte Mühle und bauten sie zu einem Museum aus. Sehenswert sind der Fachwerkbau, die Mühlenausstattung und das Birgittenmuseum.

properties.name: Corpus Christi Eschenfelden
properties.description: The "Corpus Christi" Church in Eschenfelden on Route 3 of the Simultaneous Churches Cycle Route.

properties.name: RömerMuseum Weißenburg (RomanMuseum Weißenburg)
properties.description: One of the largest treasure troves in Roman Germany can be admired at the RömerMuseum Weißenburg (RomanMuseum Weißenburg). It was probably hidden in the neighbourhood of the Great Baths in the 3rd century AD by looters collecting scrap metal. In addition to 17 statuettes of gods of varying quality from Italy and the provinces, the find also includes numerous iron artefacts and household items. The second half of the permanent exhibition focuses on the Weissenburg region in antiquity: at the time, Roman Biriciana was one of only seven equestrian forts in the province of Raetia and the seat of a Spanish equestrian unit. The ground floor of the museum houses the Limes Information Centre on the Upper Germanic-Raetian Limes in Bavaria as part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site "Frontiers of the Roman Empire".

properties.name: Kunstverein Erlangen
properties.description:
The Kunstverein Erlangen has already had its established place in Erlangen's art and cultural scene since **1904**.

In the "**New Gallery**", constantly changing **exhibitions** of painting, graphic art, sculpture, and installation showcase new trends in the art scene.

At Kunstverein Erlangen, art enthusiasts meet to take part in cultural life.

properties.name: Stadeln Indoor Pool
properties.description:
The indoor pool in the Stadeln district of Fürth

The Stadeln indoor and sports pool offers a swimming pool with a water depth of up to 2.20 meters as well as a teaching pool with a water depth of 60 to 90 centimeters. On Fridays and Saturdays, warm-water days are held, during which the water temperature is raised to 29 to 30 degrees.

properties.name: Der „Morznhof“ von Familie Alt
properties.description:
Away from the main through roads lies the little village of Seidmar. You have to find it, but anyone who has been here once is happy to come back. Seidmar lies on the Franconian Jura plateau amid mixed forests, orchards and fields. Agriculture has always played a major role here. Hiking trails lead to Walberla and Hundshaupten Wildlife Park. At the edge of the village, the orchards bloom in spring.

Right in the middle of the village, the half-timbered house of Morznhof greets visitors. The farm got its name from the nearby St. Moritz Chapel. The history of the farm and the family can be traced back to 1698. Margarete Alt likes to tell how, during the construction period, 21 carpenters spent a total of 1½ years cutting the wood for the decorative half-timbering.

**Up to ten different crops grow in the fields around Seidmar**

Her son Josef took over the farm a few years ago as a full-time farmer. “Either all in or not at all,” laughs the master farmer. Since then, he has been walking through the barn aisles, taking care of cows, bulls and calves. Right now he is pushing fresh hay toward them. He smiles contentedly: “We know what our cows get to eat; we produce the best quality.” Josef Alt grows his own feed: oats, alfalfa, corn, spring and winter barley ... up to 10 different crops grow in his fields around Seidmar. Josef Alt knows that good crop rotation and good soil are the foundation of his business. He also goes out on Sundays to check: What does the field look like? And wherever possible, he avoids using pesticides.

**A large, airy loose-housing barn**

In his newly built, airy open barn, his animals lie on straw and receive hay and silage from his own cultivation. Josef Alt breeds Simmental Fleckvieh, a breed well suited to both milk and meat production. The animals are born here and grow up here. It takes about two years until they reach slaughter maturity. Josef Alt has known each of his animals from the very beginning.

**The house specialty is beef ham smoked over hardwood**

All of this is the basis for the house specialty: Zwetschgenbaames. This slowly smoked beef ham is made “the same way it always has been,” according to a closely guarded recipe, says Margarete Alt. The recipe is passed down from generation to generation.

For the ham, the Alt family uses only the best cuts of beef. They are first cured in brine and then refined with spices and herbs. “We don’t use curing salt,” emphasizes Margarete Alt. However, the exact spice blend remains a family secret. The ham is then slowly smoked over hardwood. The special feature: the Alt family still has an old chimney, preserved in its original state, which is fired by a wood stove. This gives the ham the special aroma so appreciated by regular customers. Historians still do not entirely agree on the origin of the name Zwetschgenbaames:

Does the name come from the plum wood that, according to tradition, was once used for smoking the ham, or from the fact that after smoking the ham becomes as hard as plum wood, so that it has to be sliced as thinly as carpaccio, or does its grain after smoking resemble plum wood?

Be that as it may: Zwetschgenbaames now enjoys such a good reputation that a few years ago even the Austrian magazine Servus reported on the Alt family from Seidmar.

**The ham is available in the farm shop from September to May**

And this ham is a true regional product: from growing the feed, to raising the animals, to refining the ham — everything takes place in Seidmar. However, only from September to May; after that, it is summer break. Not only because the hay harvest needs to be handled, but also because the sun beats down on the chimney and makes smoking more difficult.

**Packed lunches for hikers**

But the Alt family prepares in advance each year and vacuum-seals a certain supply of ham, because the hikers who discover Seidmar in summer also enjoy packed lunches at the cozy farm. And sealed airtight, Zwetschgenbaames keeps for several months. By the way, Margarete Alt’s well-stocked farm shop offers not only the tasty beef ham, but also sausage and beef, pasta, eggs, jams and syrups.

And anyone planning a celebration is recommended to use [Partyservice Alt](https://partyservice-alt.de), where brother Manfred turns the farm’s fine ingredients into delicious roasts, roulades or pan dishes.

**Products directly from the farm:**

- Home-smoked Zwetschgenbames (beef ham)
- Specialties from beef and veal
- House salami
- Honey
- Pasta
- Jellies
- Rhubarb syrup
- Firewood, ready for the stove

**Special features:**

- Slaughter day is every first Friday of the month. Beef is prepared according to pre-order and individual wishes.
- Packed lunches and picnic baskets are available for hikers at any time.
- Barn tours and children’s birthday parties are organized on request.
- The farm also includes a campsite with a picnic meadow.
- The business also includes a catering service.

_Author: Corinna Brauer_

properties.name: Bio-Schäferei & Biorinderhof Familie Dorn
properties.description:
Just two kilometres from Pretzfeld lies the little village of Hagenbach. Its location in the floodplain of the Trubach stream, between orchards and hiking trails, is charming. At the entrance to the village, the old mill has stood here since the 12th century. Although the mill wheel no longer turns, the water power is still useful today and is used to generate electricity. Sheep and cattle graze in the stable and on the meadows around the house. Today, the old mill is an exemplary Naturland farm. Anyone looking for organic beef and lamb will find what they are looking for with the Dorn family.

**The farm has been in the family since 1788**

It all began with seven lambs in the family orchard. In 1996, Stefan Dorn wanted to use them to revive livestock breeding on the farm. His parents had given up cattle farming in the 1980s. Stefan Dorn was about to take over the farm, which has been in the family since 1788. And he knew that it would not stop at seven lambs. “Someday I want to have cows again,” Stefan Dorn thought to himself.

**Sheep and cattle are kept in the large open-front barn, with the pasture areas directly adjoining it**

Slowly, he began to increase his livestock. At first, the family marketed the lamb meat only within their circle of friends. As the regulations for home slaughter became increasingly strict and the number of sheep kept growing, the Dorns looked for new possibilities. Stefan Dorn leased additional land, took part in landscape conservation projects and, in 2011, made a decisive move: he became a “full-time farmer by conviction.” A new open-front barn with extensive pastureland was built on the farm. Simmental cattle moved in alongside the sheep barn. Today, 35 animals live in the spacious barn, which is bedded with a thick layer of straw. It is a pleasure to watch the animals in their herd.

**Mother-based animal rearing**

At the Dorn family farm, the animals are raised in suckler-cow husbandry, which means that the calves grow up with their mothers. They are only separated from them at the age of 10 months as “weaners.” Two calves were born tonight, and the two are still wandering around a little unsteadily. The birth of a calf is always an experience for Stefan Dorn. On some days, like today, he gets up at 2 a.m. to help twins come into the world. “When they then get up, drink and walk, I’m delighted,” says the father of three with enthusiasm, while his children romp around the farm.

**Landscape conservation with the sheep**

Stefan Dorn combines sheep and cattle farming with landscape conservation. Year after year, he leased more land and now farms over 100 hectares. During the summer season, his sheep graze on different areas on slopes, traditional orchards and solar parks. He grows the feed for his animals himself: barley, peas and oats, as well as hay and silage. All in accordance with Naturland guidelines, of course. “We don’t spray,” says Stefan Dorn. “On our farm, we don’t even have a fertilizer spreader or a grain sprayer.”

**From autodidact to livestock farmer**

Stefan Dorn taught himself the knowledge about grain cultivation from books as an autodidact; he passed the livestock farmer examination with a specialisation in sheep as an external candidate at the Triesdorf School for Animal Husbandry. Stefan Dorn turned his hobby into a profession.

He markets the meat from his animals mainly through the Naturland association. But meat packages can also be bought directly from the farm.

He has never regretted his decision to be a full-time farmer: “I would do it again anytime,” laughs Stefan Dorn, and his wife Ramona reveals the secret of their success: “We farm because we really want to. And what you enjoy doing also bears fruit.”

**Products:**

- Fresh organic beef as a package to order
- Fresh organic lamb as a package to order

**Special feature:**

- The farm is run according to Naturland guidelines.
- Slaughtering takes place 4 times a year (twice in spring and twice in autumn).

_Author: Corinna Brauer_

properties.name: Schafferhof
properties.description:
Der Hofladen bietet einen freundlichen Empfang, in der Auslage finden sich ausnahmslos hausgemachte Spezialitäten wie Bauernschinken, Leberwurst und Bauernseufzer - rund 50 verschiedene Wurstwaren!

Dazu eine beeindruckende Vielfalt an Ripple, Knöchle, Haxn und Schäufele.

Für diese Auswahl lohnt der Weg bis zum [**Schafferhof**](https://www.schafferhof.de) allemal.

Hinter der Ladentheke steht Andrea Schaffer „Ich lebe mein Hobby“, schwärmt sie.

30 Rinder und 100 Schweine stehen in den Ställen.

„Wir wollen es klein und überschaubar halten“, erzählt Andrea Schaffer.

Sie kennt ihren Mann Stefan schon aus Kindertagen, arbeitete zunächst in der Bank und stieg nach und nach in den Betrieb ihres Mannes ein.

Bereut hat sie es nie.

„Wir haben uns gesucht und gefunden“, sagt sie heute.

**Bei Familie Schaffer darf man in die Ställe schauen**

Viele ihrer Kunden wollen mittlerweile wissen, wie das Produkt erzeugt worden ist, das sie hier auf dem Hof kaufen.

Daher darf man bei Familie Schaffer gern in die Ställe schauen.

Hier stehen Angus- und Simmentaler-Rinder im Laufstall und Schweine in geräumigen Boxen auf Stroh.

Kaum jemand weiß, dass Schweine zu den klügsten Säugetieren der Welt gehören und einen ausgeprägten Spieltrieb haben.

„Das Stroh hat für unsere Schweine viele Vorteile: Sie liegen weicher, können darin wühlen, haben immer etwas zum Fressen und Spielen und sind dadurch ruhiger“, erzählt Stefan Schaffer.

Er ist Landwirt aus Leidenschaft und führt den Hof unter dem Motto „Landwirtschaft mit Herz und Verstand“.

**Für die Landwirtschaft muss man geboren sein**

„Es macht halt einfach Spaß, wenn du früh in den Stall gehst und die Tiere warten auf dich“, schwärmt Stefan Schaffer.

Und er fügt hinzu: „Du musst dafür geboren sein.“

Stefan Schaffer hat für seine Tiere geräumige Ställe eingerichtet.

„Wir sind zwar ein konventioneller Betrieb, aber die neuen Ställe sind wie für einen Biobetrieb geplant, weil wir das sowieso für gut halten“, bekräftigt er.

Die Schweine werden bei ihm so gemästet, dass sie langsam wachsen.

Statt den üblichen fünf bis sechs Monaten, haben die Tiere hier auf dem Hof zwischen sechs und zwölf Monaten Zeit bis zur Schlachtreife.

Mit 150 kg Lebendgewicht sind die Schweine von Stefan Schaffer auch schwerer, als Tiere aus konventionellen Betrieben.

**Zertifizierter Aufzucht- und Schlachtbetrieb**

Wenn sie den richtigen Schlachtzeitpunkt erreicht haben, wechseln die Tiere in den oberen Stall.

Der Schafferhof ist auch ein zertifizierter Schlachtbetrieb.

Jede Woche werden hier 5-6 Schweine geschlachtet.

Mit dem Schlachthaus hat sich Familie Schaffer ein weiteres Stück Unabhängigkeit geschaffen, auch wenn es „brutal viel Arbeit“ bedeutet.

„So wissen wir, dass es so gemacht ist, wie wir es wollen“, begründet Stefan Schaffer diese Entscheidung.

Gerade mal 10 Meter lang ist der Weg für die Schweine vom oberen Stall zum Schlachthaus.

„Bei uns wird den Tieren Zeit gegeben zu sterben“, erzählt Stefan Schaffer.

„Sie laufen aus dem Stall, schnüffeln ein bisschen und dann werden sie betäubt.“

Das Ganze dauert nur ein paar Minuten.

**Auch Getreide- und Obstanbau gehören zum Schafferhof**

Der Schafferhof ist vielseitig aufgestellt.

Neben der Schweine- und Rinderhaltung, bauen die Schaffers auch Obst und Getreide an.

Rund 60 Hektar bewirtschaften sie.

Gerste, Roggen, Mais, Hafer, Erbsen und Sonnenblumen bauen sie selbst an und schaffen damit die Futtergrundlage ihrer Tiere.

Auch Heu und Silage stammen von den eigenen Wiesen und Feldern.

Auf allen Flächen setzt Stefan Schaffer auf Zwischenfrüchte, um die Bodenqualität zu verbessern.

„Für mich ist Landwirtschaft einfach ein Gefühl, es macht mir Spaß draußen zu arbeiten, ob ganz früh oder ganz spät.

Andere Menschen fahren in den Urlaub, um das zu erleben“, erzählt Stefan Schaffer.

**700 Kirschbäume gehören zum Hof**

Rund 700 Kirschbäume gehören zum Hof, aufgrund der Sortenvielfalt dauert die Kirschenzeit hier vor den Toren Hiltpoltsteins fast bis August.

Aus ihren Äpfeln gewinnen die Schaffers fruchtigen Apfelsaft.

Zwetschgen, Birnen und Kirschen sind die Zutaten für Hochprozentiges.

**Für Gäste gibt es auch eine Ferienwohnung**

-Unterstützt werden Andrea und Stefan Schaffer von den Eltern Marianne und Alfred Schaffer.

„Wir leben hier echt im gelobten Land“, schwärmt Andrea Schaffer.

Für Gäste, die das selbst gern erleben wollen und etwas länger bleiben wollen, steht eine Ferienwohnung mit Selbstversorgung bereit.

„Wir wollen zeigen, dass man auch im Kleinen Landwirtschaft vernünftig machen kann“, sagt Andrea Schaffer.

„Vernünftig“ bedeutet für sie auch eine nachhaltige Energieversorgung mit Photovoltaik und Hackschnitzelheizung, selbst der Kochkessel im Schlachthaus wird mit Holz befeuert.

Die Landwirtschaft soll schließlich auch in der Zukunft ihren Platz hier haben.

Die junge Generation hilft schon im Stall mit.

Sieht ganz so aus, als ob die Zukunft hier schon begonnen hat.

**Besonderheiten:**

- Familie Schaffer bietet auch einen Partyservice an.
- Jeden Dienstag gibt es Kesselfleisch, frische Blut- und Leberwurst
- Jeden Freitag gibt es Hausmacher-Stadtwurst
- Jeden Freitag und Samstag außerdem Küchle, Zwiebelkuchen und Dinkelflammkuchen
- Außerdem findet man Familie Schaffer auf den Bauernmärkten in Forchheim am Paradeplatz, in Neunkirchen am Brand, in Pegnitz und in Creußen auf dem Rathausplatz.
- Sonntags verkauft Alfred Schaffer frisches Bauernbrot auf dem Parkplatz an der B2 zwischen Igensdorf und Forth.

**Produkte:**

- Rund 50 verschiedene Wurstsorten von den eigenen Strohschweinen
- Rind- und Schweinefleisch
- Kirschen
- Apfelsaft, Geiste und Brände aus Zwetschgen, Kirschen und Birnen
- Heu, Stroh
- Flammkuchen, Brot und Küchle
- Brennholz und Hackschnitzel

*Autorin: Corinna Brauer*

properties.name: Bernd Richter Farm
properties.description:
Eine gute Kartoffel hat eine glatte Schale, keine Schwarzflecken und möglichst flache Augen. Wie aber werden sie angebaut? Ein Besuch auf einem Bauernhof in Wannbach.

Bernd Richter und seine Frau Simone setzen seit vielen Jahren auf ökologische Landwirtschaft. „Ich mag einfach keine Chemie mehr spritzen oder Kunstdünger einsetzen“, sagt Bernd Richter.

**10 verschiedene Kartoffelsorten**

Der sympathische Landwirt baut auf seinen Feldern rund um Wannbach rund zehn verschiedene Kartoffelsorten an. Zu seinen Bestsellern gehören festkochende Kartoffeln wie Laura, Sieglinde oder Princess. Wer mehlige Kartoffelsorten sucht, für den ist die Sorte Lilly erste Wahl.

Ob festkochend oder mehlig – die Kartoffeln gedeihen auf den sandigen Böden zwischen Wannbach und Pretzfeld prächtig. Kartoffeln mögen keine Staunässe. Um gut zu wachsen, brauchen sie einen möglichst nährstoffreichen Boden und einen sonnigen Standort. Beim Anbau setzt Bernd Richter vor allem auf Sorten, die er früh im Jahr ernten kann. So lässt sich auch der Kartoffelkäfer im Zaum halten.

**Anhäufeln und Abstriegeln**

Damit die Kartoffeln gut anwachsen, lässt Bernd Richter seine Saatkartoffeln 2-3 Wochen vorkeimen, bevor er sie im Mai auspflanzt. „So dick wie sie sind, so viel Erde soll darüber sein“, heißt eine alte Bauernregel. Sind die Kartoffeln im Boden eingesetzt, heißt es für den Landwirt noch etwa ein bis zwei Mal die Dämme abstriegeln und wieder anhäufeln. „Danach lassen wir die Kartoffeln in Ruhe“, sagt Bernd Richter. Unkraut bekämpft der Landwirt nur maschinell: durch Hacken und Jäten.

Dank der angehäufelten Dämme erwärmt sich der Boden besser, gleichzeitig schützen die kleinen Erdwälle die lichtempfindliche Kartoffelknolle. Bekommt eine Knolle zu viel Sonne ab, bildet sie den Stoff Solanin und wird giftig. Erkennbar ist das an der grünen Farbe.

**Der richtige Erntezeitpunkt**

Von Juni bis August blüht die Kartoffel. Während der Blütezeit bildet die Kartoffel die typischen Knollen, die allmählich größer werden. Wenn die Pflanze welk und braun wird, rückt der Erntezeitpunkt näher. Zwei bis drei Wochen nach Absterben des Krautes, ist der ideale Erntezeitpunkt erreicht.

Für Bernd Richter dauert die Haupterntezeit meist von Ende Juli bis Ende September. Frühkartoffeln, die im Juli und August geerntet werden, sind noch nicht lagerfähig und müssen gleich verbraucht werden. Die lagerfähigen Kartoffeln landen im Kartoffelkeller und werden nach Sorten getrennt und in handliche 5 Kilo-Netze verpackt über die Kartoffelkiste verkauft.

Rund 50 kg Kartoffeln verbraucht ein Deutscher pro Jahr. Die Hälfte davon jedoch in Form von Pommes Frites oder ähnlich verarbeiteten Fertiggerichten. Davon ist man bei Familie Richter weit entfernt: „Wir essen die Kartoffeln am liebsten mit Schale“, erzählt der Landwirt.

**Samstags gibt es frisches Holzofenbrot**

Bernd Richter baut nicht nur Kartoffeln an – auch für das Brotbacken kann er sich begeistern. Kein Wunder: Die Tradition des Brotbackens gehört zur Gemeinde Pretzfeld wie das Kirschenfest im Juli. „Bei uns auf dem Hof wurde schon immer Brot gebacken“, erzählt der Landwirt.

Er verarbeitet jede Woche 50 - 60 Kilogramm Mehl zu frischem Sauerteigbrot. Auf Wunsch verfeinert er es mit Walnüssen oder Röstzwiebeln. Schon sein Vater war begeisterter Brotbäcker. Als der alte Backofen baufällig wurde, errichtete Bernd Richter einen neuen Holzofen. Ihm war es wichtig, die alte Tradition fortzuführen.

**Der Backtag beginnt morgens um 4 Uhr**

Damit das Brot am Samstag fertig ist, beginnt Bernd Richter bereits am Freitagmittag mit den Vorbereitungen. Mehrmals füttert er seinen Sauerteigansatz mit Mehl an, um die Teigkulturen zu aktivieren. Samstags ist Bernd Richter bereits ab 4 Uhr morgens auf den Beinen, um den Teig zu verarbeiten. Das kräftige Durchkneten übernimmt heute bei ihm die Knetmaschine. Wenn am Morgen die Laibe geformt und eingeschossen werden, hilft auch Ehefrau Simone mit. Ab 11:30 Uhr ist alles zum Verkauf bereit.

Zum Betrieb von Bernd Richter gehören auch einige Streuobstbestände mit Äpfeln, Birnen und Kirschen. „Landwirtschaft ist für mich ein körperlicher Ausgleich. Es macht mir Spaß zu sehen, dass was wächst“, erzählt der Landwirt.

Das Streuobst lässt er in der [Kleinbrennerei Rackelmann in Hundshaupten](https://www.die-kleinbrennerei.de/) versaften: „Es ist einfach schön, wenn du dabei bist und auch mal einen faulen Apfel aussortieren kannst.“ Landwirtschaft bedeutet für Familie Richter auch die Fortführung einer Tradition: „Der Ort ist da“, sagt Bernd Richter. Und er will ihn auch für zukünftige Generationen erhalten. „Es ist eine schöne Arbeit“, lacht der Landwirt. „Ich bin einfach gern draußen in der Natur.“

**Besonderheiten:**

- Jede Woche backt Bernd Richter frisches Holzofenbrot. Bestellung bis Freitag, Abholung am Samstag zwischen 11:30 und 16 Uhr.
- Kartoffeln können jederzeit in der Kartoffelkiste am Hof abgeholt werden.

**Produkte:**

- Holzofenbrot natur oder mit Röstzwiebeln und Walnüssen auf Vorbestellung
- Apfelsaft und Obstbrände vom eigenen Streuobst

*Autorin: Corinna Brauer*

properties.name: Erlwein Fruit Farm
properties.description:
“Even now, you still need a good plum for a plum cake,” Herbert Erlwein says with a smile as his gaze wanders over the long rows of fruit trees. His farm is in Ermreus, a small village off the main roads that belongs to the municipality of Kunreuth. To get to his orchard, Herbert Erlwein only has to step outside.

**Peaches and grapes also thrive in the Ermreus orchards**

Around his farm, spicy Santana apples, aromatic peaches, cherries, grapes and apricots grow in gently curving rows. Many old varieties are among them, such as the “Butterbirne” or the “Köstliche von Charneux,” because they are more aromatic and less susceptible to pests. Between his trees, Herbert Erlwein has created numerous nesting places for tits, bees and bumblebees. At the edges stand hedges of blackthorn, rose hips and hawthorn. At the beginning of each row of trees, Herbert Erlwein has planted a rose bush. “I just like roses,” he laughs. Always in view: the Hetzles Mountain.

**Herbert Erlwein planted thousands of fruit trees**

“I’ve been fascinated by fruit trees since I was a child,” Herbert Erlwein says. Agriculture always played an important role in his family. The history of the old farmstead can be traced back to the 17th century. Herbert Erlwein became a master gardener and specialized in fruit growing. When he took over the farm from his father, he first thoroughly reorganized it: he sold the old farmstead, gave up pigs, cattle and chickens, and built a new farm on the edge of the village with plenty of space for fruit trees. He planted thousands of trees; after four years came the first yield, and after ten years he was able to make a living from it. Today he farms 11 hectares full-time.

**13 different crops grow in the orchards**

Traditional orchard meadows are part of it too. “A loose stand of trees like that is simply beautiful to look at,” enthuses the friendly master gardener. Twice a year he mows the meadows under the trees; otherwise he leaves them in peace. His main source of income is the fruit from his orchards. The trees there are on average 25 years old. There is plenty to do here all year round. Pruning begins in February and March. Expertise is needed here so that the 13 different crops each receive their individual pruning. In April and May, when the trees are in full bloom, Herbert Erlwein is in his orchards every day. Then intuition and experience are important: he has to assess, observe and make decisions. For example, about the use of fungicides. If warm, humid weather persists for a longer period, there is a risk of scab infection. Then Herbert Erlwein has to intervene, even though he would prefer to avoid spraying. “Otherwise I can throw away my harvest. Even organic farming doesn’t work without plant protection.”

**What a variety of fruit!**

In June, when the first apples ripen, it is time for Herbert Erlwein to thin the crop. To ensure that the apples grow as large as possible, small and scabbed apples are sorted out. At the beginning of June, the harvest season starts with the first cherries. In July come the first peaches and apricots, in August the apples and plums. The fruit is carefully “pulled” from the tree so that it does not get bruised. Herbert Erlwein is supported by a small team of harvest helpers. Herbert Erlwein picks a tree up to three times, because the fruit ripens at different rates. Herbert Erlwein wants to offer his customers fully ripened fruit so that they can taste the subtle differences between the varieties.

**The farm shop is open on Fridays and Saturdays**

From the very beginning, Herbert Erlwein relied on direct marketing. Over the years, he built up a considerable customer base. Ermreus’s secluded location is deceptive: on Fridays and Saturdays there is a steady stream of visitors coming and going at the farm. It has long since become known that you can buy an impressive variety of fresh fruit here. Depending on the season, there are strawberries, peaches, plums, apricots, blueberries, currants, apples, pears, grapes, quinces and walnuts.

**Fruit growers with heart and soul**

The Erlweins are fruit growers through and through. Herbert Erlwein also uses his direct line to customers to inform them about fruit growing. He emphasizes: “Our nature and landscape are dear to us all, worth living in and therefore worth preserving. They are shaped by human hands. Yet nature is not static; it cannot be forced into a corset of laws and regulations. We live and work with nature; the fruits of our trees are our daily bread.”

**Wife Hilde Wöhrmann is responsible for the variety of products in the farm shop**

The good soul of the farm shop is his wife, Hilde Wöhrmann. The fruit that Herbert Erlwein harvests is transformed by Hilde, with great imagination, into vinegars, syrups and fruit spreads. This produces, for example, a red apple jelly. “There isn’t a gram of coloring in it,” Hilde Wöhrmann laughs. It is the red flesh of the Baya Marisa variety alone that gives the apple jelly its red color. Particularly popular are Hilde’s quince and apple vinegars. “Our apple vinegar is now 12 years old; nothing has been added to it,” says the warm-hearted host. She even turns medlars, rose hips and quinces into fruit spreads, even though, as she says, these fruits are already “extreme” in terms of preparation.

**Fruit spreads are made by hand**

Cooking is still true handcraft for Hilde Wöhrmann. “I stir it myself because I need to feel the fruit. Sometimes a fruit is a little sweeter, then I don’t need to add as much sugar. But you only notice that when stirring by hand,” she explains. The marinated cheese is made the same way: “That keeps me busy for at least three hours,” she laughs. “When my customers then say, ‘That tasted great again, do you have any more of it?’, that makes me happy.”

**There are also insect drinkers, cloth bags and woven shopping baskets in the farm shop**

To surprise her customers, Hilde Wöhrmann is constantly looking for new ideas. She has expanded the range in her shop not only to include marinated cheese. Since August, there have also been products made from Franconian carp from a nearby family smokehouse. And anyone still looking for a suitable gift will find stylish insect drinkers, colorful cloth bags and woven shopping baskets.

**Special features:**

- The Erlweins’ farm also includes an apple festival, which takes place once a year on the farm.
- Hilde Wöhrmann also plays a leading role in the Ermaser Madla association, which shapes the cultural life of the small community. [Here’s the article!](https://www.infranken.de/lk/gem/ermreus-und-seine-madla-art-5078235)

**Products:**

- Fresh fruit depending on the season: strawberries, peaches, plums, apricots, blueberries, currants, apples, pears, grapes, quinces and walnuts
- Fruit vinegars, fruit spreads, syrups also made from rose hips, medlars and quinces
- smoked carp mousse and smoked carp from a friend’s carp farm
- marinated cheese
- handicrafts from small businesses in the area

*Author: Corinna Brauer*

properties.name: Gath Zebu Farm
properties.description:
*Egg liqueur, chicken and turkey from organic farming, eleven different kinds of vinegar and cheese from the Aischgrund … there are many reasons to visit the farm shop of the Gath family in Weilersbach. But the most important one is probably the delicate meat of the zebu cattle. “Zebu” comes from the Tibetan “ceba” and means hump.*

Small, sure-footed and humped - that is zebu cattle. “Zebu cattle are a robust breed that calve well and rarely get sick,” Christian Gath sums up. Together with his wife Manuela, he keeps around 70 animals of this special breed. Zebus are among the smallest cattle in the world. They are descended from the aurochs, have a calm, frugal nature and are considered very undemanding. That makes them so important for landscape maintenance, because zebu cattle are content with anything that grows in the pasture. Due to their delicate build and light weight, they also leave hardly any hoof damage. This makes them the ideal choice for grazing the slopes around Weilersbach. The light-footed breed is also ideally suited to the much-vaunted dual use of orchard meadows: at the Gath family’s farm, the zebus graze between the farm’s own apple and pear trees.

**Almost year-round grazing**

The almost year-round grazing has a very positive effect on the meat quality: meat from zebu cattle is very fine-grained, dark, and tastes a little like game. In the Gath family’s farm shop, zebu beef is therefore available not only as steak or goulash, but also as burger patties or bratwurst.

**Plum Bames from zebu beef**

One specialty is the plum Bames made from zebu beef. Behind the term “Zwetschgenbames” lies a raw beef ham that acquires its typical reddish-brown color through slow smoking. At Christian Gath’s, the firm beef ham, for which only the finest cuts are used, comes in three different varieties: cured in brine, refined with paprika and chili, or with seasoned pepper.

**A living room became a farm shop**

It all began in 2007 with 4 animals that Manuela and Christian Gath had been given as a gift. The Gaths quickly became enthusiastic about the small, frugal cattle with the distinctive hump, and the herd grew. “When it was slaughter day and we were selling, we had to take two weeks off. After that we were completely exhausted,” Christian Gath laughs. Slowly, the decision matured to give agriculture more space. Production and sales were to be put on a professional footing. The former grandparents’ house of Manuela Gath was quickly converted: where the living room once was, there is now a small, stylish farm shop. The range includes not only the various zebu products, but also turkey and chicken meat, eggs from the farm’s own free-range husbandry, and cheeses from the Aisch Valley. “We also wanted to offer something for vegetarians,” Manuela Gath laughs. Their selection of fruit and herb vinegars is also impressive: at least 11 varieties of vinegar are always in stock, for example apple, pear, blackberry, strawberry, cherry, peach, quince, mirabelle plum or lemon balm. Customers who bring their own container can fill it themselves.

**Every animal has a name**

By now, the herd of zebu cattle has grown to 70 animals. Instead of year-round grazing, the zebus spend the winter in a modern loose housing barn, and instead of five hectares of land, Christian Gath now farms 30 hectares. “Every animal still has a name with us,” Christian Gath emphasizes, pointing to the pasture where “Susi,” his oldest zebu cow, is chewing contentedly. She is almost nineteen years old. “Watching the zebus graze in the pastures simply does me good,” he laughs.

At this point, a few more animals should be mentioned, because the Gath family also keeps 40 chickens, 15 turkeys, 80 geese and 160 broiler chickens on their farm - all organic. Christian Gath grows wheat, barley and field beans himself. Even if that means a lot of work: “For me, it’s simply my balance,” he laughs and looks gratefully at his wife. Here in Weilersbach, landscape maintenance, organic farming and creative marketing go hand in hand.

Open: Friday from 4-7 p.m. and Saturday from 10 a.m.-1 p.m. or by telephone appointment

**Products:**

- Chicken (whole or halved)
- Turkey (whole or halved)
- Chicken breast and leg
- Turkey breast and leg
- Various sausages on rotation (salami, Polish sausage, pepper sticks, meat sausage, ham sausage, Göttinger, Vienna sausages and cheese sausages)
- Plum Bames from zebu beef
- Pollo Fino – meat removed from chicken legs, ideal for grilling
- Geese
- Meat from zebu cattle
- Burger patties from zebu beef
- Apple and pear juice from the farm’s own orchard meadows
- Fruit, berry and herb vinegars (at least 11 different varieties)

*Author: Corinna Brauer*

properties.name: Distler Sheep Farm & Juralamm Producers’ Association
properties.description:
*__Landscape conservation that tastes good!__*

Delicate green herbs are making their way through the leaf litter; spring has turned the barren slopes into an herb garden. Here, where the rocks are within sight, lies the refuge of Georg Distler and his around 500 breeding ewes. Their bleating can be heard far and wide, mingling with the birdsong. Shepherding is a relic of times gone by: in the past, there was a shepherd in almost every village. Today, there are only a few left throughout the Franconian Switzerland region, and in Bavaria there are only around 80 professional shepherds.

**Georg Distler is one of 80 migratory shepherds in Bavaria**

One of them is Georg Distler from Egloffstein. From May until the onset of winter, he is on the move with his flocks of sheep, grazing the herb-rich slopes at Ehrenbürg, in the Trubach Valley, or around Egloffstein. The four-legged woolly helpers climb slopes and rocks effortlessly to nibble ribwort plantain, coltsfoot, and wild thyme. “My animals have a wonderful life,” Georg Distler laughs. As shepherd and sheep move from meadow to meadow, they are accompanied by the herding dog, which makes sure the sheep do not simply wander off on their own. As soon as the shepherd gives a command, the dog races off and drives the sheep back to the flock.

**Many breeding successes with Merino land sheep**

Georg Distler mainly breeds Merino land sheep. “We want to deliver proper meat,” the shepherd emphasizes. That is why he is often out with his sheep in winter too, grazing harvested fields that friendly farmers have made available to him. Unfortunately, it is becoming increasingly difficult for him as well to find suitable areas for his sheep.

“We work here like in the Middle Ages,” the likeable farmer laughs. As he says, he was “born into” the shepherd’s profession. His day begins at 5:30 a.m. and rarely ends before 9 p.m. As a shepherd, he is not only a farmer and landscape manager, but ideally also a butcher and marketing manager who sells the animals’ meat himself.

**Shepherds are indispensable for landscape conservation and the linking of biotopes**

The work of shepherds is indispensable for landscape conservation. In particular, dry grasslands and juniper heaths need the help of grazing animals, because if the areas are not grazed, they become overgrown with scrub within 5 or 10 years. Meadows and heaths are true hotspots of biodiversity and are usually found on slopes and remote high plateaus that have become uneconomical for agricultural use. Yet it is precisely here that there is a refuge for heat-loving plant and animal species such as the great pasque flower, yellow broomrape, and cypress spurge. They have adapted to the harsh living conditions and cope very well with extreme heat, drought, and strong winds. Sheep also play an important role in linking biotopes: [researchers at the Institute for Agroecology in Neustadt an der Weinstraße](https://www.domaene-oppenheim.de/Internet/global/themen.nsf/0/CC1D17E2BFF04450C12585CE002A0F0F/$FILE/200824_Abschlussbericht%20EIP-Vorhaben_Vernetzung%20verinselter%20Biotope%20-%20Biodiversitätstaxis%202.0.pdf) have found that a flock of 500 sheep can transport up to 2 million plant seeds in its wool. Sheep therefore not only help graze species-rich dry grasslands, but also help spread the richness and diversity of plant populations. Funding for landscape conservation and agri-environment schemes therefore now makes up the largest share of a shepherd’s income.

**Migratory shepherds do not need fences**

What distinguishes landscape conservation with sheep from that with grazing cattle? “What is special about the shepherd is that he moves freely with his animals and maintains landscapes without interfering with nature,” explains Martin Barthl, managing director of the [Bavarian Sheep Farmers’ Association](https://www.alpinetgheep.com/verbaende.html). “Unlike grazing cattle, for which fences first have to be built, the shepherd leaves nature as it should be, without building over it,” he adds. For Martin Barthl, being a shepherd is a dream job, “but first you have to be able to afford this profession,” he laughs.

**Quality wool has now become a waste product**

Rather than living off landscape conservation, shepherds would much prefer to live off what their sheep produce: wool and meat. But wool, which has been bred for quality for centuries, no longer generates any income today. “Shearing sheep is hardly profitable anymore. The proceeds from sheep’s wool don’t even cover the shearer’s working time,” says Martin Barthl. The current wool price is 0.50 euros per kilogram. To at least cover the working time of shearers and helpers, shepherds would need a wool price of 6 euros per kilogram.

**The price of lamb has been falling for years**

The price of lamb has also been below the world market price for years. Although sheep are part of the cultural landscape and the image of the low mountain ranges, lamb consumption is declining. Suitable slaughterhouses are not always available near the sheep farms. “It makes no sense for sheep to be transported all over Germany for slaughter,” says managing director Martin Barthl from Munich.

**Animal welfare in its perfect form**

Martin Barthl therefore describes Georg Distler’s farm in Egloffstein as an example of “animal welfare in its perfect form.” The sheep spend most of their lives on the meadows of Franconian Switzerland, are bred for hardiness, and therefore do not need antibiotics. What is special is that Georg Distler is also a master butcher and slaughters his animals directly on the farm. Years ago he invested in his own slaughter rooms and markets his meat through the Juralamm producers’ association to regional butcher shops, restaurateurs, and private customers.

**The lamb meat is available to order direct from the farm**

The lambs are usually four to six months old when they are slaughtered. There are three to four lambing periods per year. Slaughter takes place to order, and the meat is cut ready for the kitchen — guaranteeing excellent quality. Around Easter, there can be as many as 120 animals. Otherwise, Georg Distler works to order.

**Lamb is exceptionally healthy and low in calories**

By the way, lamb scores not only in landscape conservation; it is also exceptionally healthy. It contains high-quality protein, hardly any carbohydrates, and important vitamins and minerals. It is also very low in calories.

**South German migratory and herding sheep farming is UNESCO intangible cultural heritage**

For Martin Barthl of the [Bavarian Sheep Farmers’ Association](https://www.alpinetgheep.com/verbaende.html), lamb is the ideal combination of landscape conservation and the production of a high-quality food. It is no wonder that UNESCO has designated South German migratory and herding sheep farming as intangible cultural heritage. As sheep farms decline, knowledge about herding and guiding sheep, about keeping and breeding the animals, and not least about using grazing land, is disappearing too — and with it the cultural landscape as we know and value it.

**Juralamm Producers’ Association e.V., Distler family**

Markgrafenstr. 94a, 91349 Egloffstein

Tel. 09197 - 207

**Special features:**

- Lamb roast is available from many butchers in the region. A sheep up to one year old is considered “lamb”; “milk lambs” are particularly young animals that have not yet eaten grass. The older the animals, the more intense or “stronger” the flavor. Many consumers therefore prefer the meat of young animals.

**You can buy and enjoy Juralamm here:**

- Lamm Butcher Shop, Pretzfeld
- [Trautner Butcher Shop, Kirchehrenbach](https://www.walberla.de/users/35/114/metzgerei-trautner.html) LINK
